title: Chapter 22 – What a Mother Doesn't Ask
html:
[Lin Clan – Su Qinghe]

She does not ask the second time.

She watches her son stand in the starlight with his mouth open and no answer in it, and she lets the silence run until it becomes its own kind of reply. Then she says, "Go to sleep," in the voice she uses for the weather, and he goes. His new boots make no sound on the frozen mud. At the turn of the terrace wall he stops, and she thinks that he will say something, and he does not. He goes on.

Su Qinghe stands alone by the ruined kiln for a long time.

Twenty-four years ago, a girl of fifteen sat at the back of a firelit cave and learned which man in her father's band had taken coin to lead him into the den of a fourth-rank beast. It is a thing she carries the way other women carry a ring. She has never forgotten what it felt like to know. She has also never forgotten the lesson that came with it, which was not about betrayal at all.

It was about how little a person wants to be asked.

You can know a thing for years, she thinks, and say nothing, and it will cost you less than the day you ask and are told.

She takes a breath of cold air. Then she turns toward the house, and goes to bed, and lies awake until the first gray touches the shutter.

* * *

At dawn she takes a washing basket down to the lowest terrace.

It is the most natural thing in the world. A woman of the Lin household going down to the stream with a load of wet linen is as unremarkable as a hen. She wears her oldest jacket, with her sleeves rolled and her hair tied in a rag, and she hums as she goes, a thing she has not done in years and is startled to find she still can. At the stream she kneels, plunges a sheet into the cold water, and lays two fingers on the cloth.

Frostfinger Palm, the compendium calls it, a Mortal-rank art she learned at nineteen from a Sea-road laundress who had no idea she was teaching a killer. A thin sheet of chill runs along the fabric. The water in the weave goes to ice for the space of a breath, cracks free, and falls away in a spray of white flakes, and the sheet comes out of the stream dry and stiff and smelling of snow. The women of the Hollow use it to wring a week's washing in an hour. Su Qinghe has used it, from time to time, to break a man's wrist.

She hangs the sheet over a rope. She does the same with the next. And when the basket is half empty, and the dawn has cleared the ridge, and nobody on the terraces above is watching a woman wash, she walks twenty paces along the bank to the old brick kiln, and sets down her load, and sits on the wall with her back to the north.

She does not turn. She does not need to. She puts one hand behind her, flat against the bricks, as casually as a woman steadying herself, and finds the four that are loose.

They are exactly as he left them. That is the first thing. Whoever put them back did it with a care she recognizes: not a fingerprint out of place, the mortar dust brushed into the seam. A thief's care. She is not surprised to learn that her son has it. She is surprised to learn how it feels.

She works out the bricks one at a time and lays them in her lap, in order.

The bag is oilcloth, double-waxed, tied with a cord. She opens it far enough to see. Silver gleams in the dark. She does not count it. She does not need to; she can tell the weight of a bag of stones by the way the cord bites, and this one is two hundred and some, with three heavier ones lying like seeds at the bottom. A ledger, bound in blue cloth. A letter.

She reads the letter.

It is on good paper, folded in thirds, sealed with red wax that has been broken and re-pressed. The crest is a jagged ridge beneath a rising sun. She has seen it twice before, once on a petition, and once on the door of a house in Willow Ford where a man had been killed. It is the crest of Red Ridge.

The hand is neat, controlled, and very polite. It is not Zhao Heng's own; he does not write such letters. It is the hand of someone who writes for him.

To the Steward of Green Pine Hill, with the compliments of the Zhao family.

We understand that the Patriarch of your house intends, at midsummer, a matter of some delicacy. We take no position on it. We observe only that whatever its outcome, the hill will need a master who values good neighbors. The Zhao family would be glad to see that master be yourself. On the day of that outcome, whichever it may be, the matter of your obligations to our house shall be considered closed.

She reads it three times. On the third she finds that her hand, holding the paper, is perfectly steady and perfectly cold.

Whatever its outcome. Not a word about death. Not a word about harm. A letter that a magistrate might read without a flicker, and that every person who knows how to read it would understand at once.

Midsummer. It is still weeks away, and the date has been spoken in only one room. Su Qinghe folds the letter along its old creases and puts it back where it was. She replaces the bag, and the bricks, one at a time, and wipes the mortar dust into the seam with the side of her thumb. Then she lifts her basket and carries it back up the hill, humming.

She has not decided what she feels. She has decided what she will do.

* * *

She had not meant to go into the cave.

That is a lie, and she knows it is a lie, and it is not the sort she tells herself often. She had meant to go into it from the moment Feng came down from the cliff that dawn, with his lamp-black face, and said in a flat voice that the Vulture was dead and that a boy had done it. She had gone in with Kai and Dong behind her, because that was the order Feng gave. But she had gone first.

She remembers it with great clarity.

The ice door lay open. The passage beyond was warm and wet and stank of old blood. The round chamber was black and cold, the lamp lay in ruins in the center of the basin, and the basin itself, a long coil of stone channels, was full of congealed black-red glue. On the floor in the middle, flat on his face, was the dead man.

She had looked at him for a long time. He had been a thin, middle-aged man, with a ruined eye, and a mouth that even in death seemed about to say something clever. Her own knife was in his side. She had pulled it out with a sound she still hears.

Then she had looked at the floor.

There are things a hunter learns to read before she learns to read letters. A mud print on a stone. A broken thread. A drip of sap on the underside of a leaf. The floor of that chamber was a book she could read as fast as she could breathe. Gu Yan's marks were everywhere, the heavy, dragging steps of a man who had run until he could not. And running through them, light and quick and only a hand's breadth apart, a second set.

Small. A child's. Narrow-heeled and soft-soled, with a long crack across the left heel.

She had known the boots. She had stitched them. The old pair, the ones she had meant to burn in the winter and had instead put at the back of the wardrobe, and which Jian, being Jian, had taken from the wardrobe without asking.

The prints went to the edge of the basin. They went around it. They went to a pillar, and to a spot beside the pillar where the stone had been scraped bright. They went to the dead man's side and stopped. They went to a notch in the rim of the coil, and she bent down to look at it, and in the notch, driven deep, with its head tuned to the faint blue sheen of well-made iron, was a pin.

It was no ordinary pin. She had seen a hundred of Hu's, and a few of Jian's flawed ones, with their careful seventy-eight percent. This was neither. The groove was cut to the hair. The head was dressed with such patience that it caught the light like a mirror. It was the work of a craftsman, of a kind that exists perhaps once in a hundred years, and it was not Hu's.

She had stood there with her fingers on it and understood three things at once.

Her son had killed a Foundation Establishment cultivator. Her son had made, in secret, a thing better than the best smith in the valley. And Kai's voice was coming down the passage behind her, saying, Aunt? Aunt, is it safe?

She had pulled the pin out and put it in her sleeve.

She had knelt, as if to examine the body, and with the flat of her hand she had smoothed away every small bootprint from the nearest stone: from the pillar, the basin, the corpse. It had taken her nineteen breaths. When Kai and Dong came in, they found a woman kneeling by a dead man, and a floor that told no story at all.

The pin is in her bedroom now, in a tin box under the floorboard. She has not looked at it since.

When Old Hu came into the cave an hour later, leaning on his rod, he had looked at the floor. Then at her. His one eye rested on her face for a very long moment, and she met it, and saw that he had seen exactly what she had seen. Neither of them had said a word.

Later, in the courtyard, he had paused beside her. "You are very good with a broom, Qinghe," he said, and went on.

She had not forgotten it.

* * *

She keeps a list. She has never written it down.

It is a long list now. It has been growing since her son was three years old, and she could recite every item in the dark. A willow bark he knew how to sweeten before anyone taught him. A press that worked on a principle no one in the Hollow could name. The stele in the old tomb, and its five dim lights, and the way he had looked at them as though they were an old friend. A deed that appeared under the founder's stand, in the place only a child could reach, after a month in which Jian had gone about the library with an expression of great and innocent concentration. A bag of stones in the dark, described to the stone.

Seven items. There are more. The tally on her own body, in the mornings, of the times he has lied to her without a flicker, and the thousand times he has told her the truth in a way that was not quite true. The way he looks at Hu. The way he looks at his father's hands. The way, on a certain winter night, he looked at the hair of a dead rogue and said, quite calmly, I am sorry, Mother, but I think the knife is the wrong shape.

She does not know what her son is. She has stopped pretending she does. What she knows is what he does, and what it costs, and who it keeps alive.

She knows what a secret is for. She has carried enough of them. A secret is not a lie. A secret is a door with a person standing behind it, and the only thing that keeps it shut is that nobody leans on it. If she asks him, he will tell her, because he is a good boy, and then it will be a thing two people know, and then three, and then a thing the Zhao can find in her face.

The only protection a secret has, she thinks, is that no one asks.

So she will not ask. She will be what she has always been, a plain, tired, watchful woman with a knife, who is a little handy and a little too quiet. She will be the wall. She will let the hill credit her cunning with every impossible thing that comes out of her son's head, and she will smile when they do, and the day he is ready to put his hand on the latch and tell her himself, she will be sitting on the other side of the door.

It is not much of a plan. It is the only one she has ever trusted.

* * *

The meditation chamber lies beneath the stone hut at the back of the compound, down forty worn steps, in a stillness that makes the ears ring. Su Qinghe has been down only twice. The air on the stairs is warm and heavy and tastes of coins. At the bottom, in a round room carved from the living rock, a lamp burns before a low black cushion, and on the cushion, with his back to her, sits Lin Zhenshan, Patriarch of the Lin clan, a hundred and sixteen years old.

He does not turn. "You've been to the kiln."

"Yes, Father."

"And?"

She tells him. The bag, the stones, the ledger, the letter. She tells him the words of the letter, as near as she remembers them, and she watches the old man's shoulders as she does. They do not move. At the end, he sits for a long time.

"Whatever its outcome," he says at last.

"Yes."

"They have never written me a threat. Not in sixty years. A man who writes a threat can be summoned before the Hall. A man who writes the hill will need a master cannot." He sighs. "It is a very good letter. I wonder who taught him."

"Zhao Heng does not write his own."

"No. He has a clerk for that. A clever one." Grandfather turns, finally, and his old gray eyes are very steady. "Qinghe. I will tell you what I intend, and you will tell me where I'm a fool."

He lays it out simply. He speaks to her as he does to Wenyuan, a general to a captain, plainly, without pity and without pride.

He will not expose his steward. Not yet. The Compact is a cage for both sides. A tributary patriarch who strikes his own steward without a council judgment hands Zhao an accusation: tyrant, in the language of the Outer Affairs Hall, and a petition for arbitration over the hill. And if he does it before the pill arrives, Zhao will not wait for midsummer. Zhao Heng will do what he has been waiting sixty years to do, and he will do it under the cover of that arbitration, in the weeks while a Lin Patriarch is distracted by his own house.

"So Wenhai stays," says Su Qinghe.

"Wenhai stays. He sits at the table. He writes in his book. He believes he is clever, and he is, and we let him believe it." The old man's mouth twists. "A leak that you know about is a better weapon than any I have forged. I will pour what I choose into it. He will carry it to Zhao like a bucket."

"And the date?"

"Midsummer. I will let him believe he has taken it from me by cunning. He will tell Zhao. Zhao will come when I have decided he should." A pause. "Not before."

"And when he comes?"

"He will come as he always comes, by the book." Grandfather's voice is dry. "There is a clause in the Compact, Qinghe, that has been waiting for a house like mine for four hundred years. If a tributary patriarch dies with no heir confirmed by the Hall, a neighboring elder who holds a petition from a member of the family may enter, for three days, to keep order. I have lodged Wenyuan's name with the Hall. It will be recorded at the autumn session. Not before."

She understands. "A window."

"A window the size of a season. And in the middle of it, a house with its Patriarch sealed in the chamber, a steward with a petition in his pocket, and a neighbor of great virtue who finds himself, quite naturally, called upon." He folds his hands. "He will come to keep order. He will find a family waiting for him."

"With what?"

"With what we have been making all spring." He lifts one finger. "Pins. Plates. Rings. Every gate and wall and well. Hu and the boy, setting them in the dark. Twelve in a circle around this hut. Nine under the road. I charge the plates myself, every night, with the vein under my hand." He shows her his palm. It is gray, like a man's hand after a long fever. "And the people."

"I have them drilling."

"I know. I have watched." He nods slowly. "Wenshi's militia with the Sect's mortal-rank steel, the relics from the armory, the Azure Sword, the Silent Spear. Not much against a cultivator. Enough to hold a door. Feng's cousins with their Flame-Bursts and Ramparts. Wenqing's pills. Your Tidal Spear. Hu's rod." He smiles very slightly. "It is not an army. It is a family that remembers how to be cunning."

She says nothing. She is looking at the lamp, and at the shadow it throws, long and wavering, across the rock.

"And the pill," she says.

"Will be delivered sealed, by Mo's hands, to Wenhai's, to mine. It will not leave this chamber again until I eat it." He looks at her directly. "If the steward means to touch it, he will touch it in front of the whole family, on the day it arrives, in the hall. I will see to that."

"You have a plan to catch him."

"I have a plan to let him be caught." The old eyes are very kind. "It is a different thing. You were always a better judge of that than my sons."

She bows. It is not a bow she gives often.

On the steps going up, she thinks: He is a hundred and sixteen years old, and he is going to put his life on a pill that the one man who handles it wants him dead. And he has not once, in the whole conversation, asked me to be afraid for him.

She finds that her eyes are stinging, and puts it down to the lamp.

* * *

She follows Wenhai that evening.

It is not difficult. He is a man of habits, and one of them is a walk. Every third dusk since the storm, he has gone out through the east gate with a hand lantern and a book under his arm, to take the air, as he says to the guards, and be alone with his figures. He walks very slowly. He does not look behind him.

She takes the long way, over the ridge above the road, through the cedars, and she goes in the soft-soled shoes she wore in the islands, with a Wind-Veil slip tucked under her collar to bend the sound of her step. It is a good talisman. Jian's father drew it. It makes her, for a space of thirty paces, no more than a movement in the grass.

The old shrine stands in a pine clearing, half an hour from the wall. It is a thing so ancient that the road to it has grown over. A moss-tiled roof on four crooked posts, a stone platform, and on the platform a faceless earth god, worn by rain to a gray lump. Nobody has made an offering there in thirty years. It is the sort of place a man goes to meet someone he is not supposed to meet.

Wenhai arrives first. He sits on the step and waits, with his lantern between his feet.

Twenty minutes later, a second man comes up the path from the east.

She knows him by his walk before she sees his face: a long, loose, arrogant stride, with the right shoulder carried a little forward, like a man who has never in his life had to step aside. Zhao Qian. He is twenty, and handsome in the cold way of his house, and he wears a gray-green robe that has never seen a day's work. He carries nothing. He does not sit.

She lies in the pines forty paces off, with her cheek on the needles, and turns the small shell in her palm until its mouth faces the shrine.

It is a Listening Shell. A Yellow Grade artifact, no larger than a thumbnail, that she took off a dead river-pirate on the Eastern Sea, and has used maybe a dozen times. It gathers sound the way a cupped hand gathers water. What it brings her now is thin and a little tinny, but clear.

"...cannot be done, Young Master." Wenhai's voice. Unsteady, but not unkind. "The deed was in the tube. I took the tube. I brought it to your grandfather myself. Then it was found. In the hall. Under the founder's tablet, where a child could reach it. I swear to you on my ancestors, I do not know how."

"You do not know," says Zhao Qian.

"I do not."

"Then you have no value to us."

A long, long silence. The pines creak. Su Qinghe watches Wenhai's hands, which are folded in his lap, and which have begun to tremble.

"I have the date," he says. "I have the date of the attempt. I have the names of the two men on the east gate. I have the layout of the pins on the road, as much as I can see. I have—"

"We have the date." Zhao Qian's voice is almost bored. "Midsummer. The longest day. Did you think the old man's pill was a secret? He bought it with Hu's iron. All Willow Ford knows it." He tilts his head. "What my grandfather wants to know is whether the steward of Green Pine can be depended upon to do a small thing."

"What thing?"

Zhao Qian reaches into his sleeve. He takes out a little paper packet no bigger than a thumb, folded in the Sect's pale green wrapping, and holds it out, between two fingers, so the lantern light catches it.

"It is a pinch of dust. It has no taste. It has no smell. It is harmless to a man who sits still. It is a kindness, Steward, for a very old man who has been brave long enough." He smiles. "It does one thing only. When a cultivator draws in the full surge of a breakthrough, it makes the heart stop for the length of one breath. That is all. One breath. And the foundation shatters. He is too old. It would have happened anyway."

Su Qinghe stops breathing.

"You want me," Wenhai says. His voice has gone very small. "To poison the Patriarch."

"I want you to touch a pill." Zhao Qian lays the packet on the step beside him, and straightens. "A pinch on the outside. On the day you carry it up the hill. You will not even be in the room when it happens. And on that day, whatever happens, your debts are closed, your position is secure, and when the Lins have need of a master, there will be one who understands good neighbors." He turns to go. "Or, of course, there is the other way. The deed. The arbiter. The ledger you keep at the kiln. My grandfather is a patient man. He has not yet decided which of us you are."

He walks away through the pines.

Wenhai sits for a long time with the lantern between his feet and the packet beside him. Su Qinghe sees him lift his hands to his face. She sees his shoulders begin to shake. He is weeping, without sound, the way a man weeps who has been weeping alone for years, and when he is done, he reaches out with a hand that does not seem to belong to him, and takes the packet, and puts it in the cuff of his left sleeve.

She waits until his lantern has gone a long way down the path.

Then she goes home by the high ridge, in the dark, without the Veil, and without a sound, and for the whole of the way she does not feel her feet touch the ground.

* * *

She finds Lin Jian on the threshing floor, an hour before midnight.

He is practicing. He does it most nights now, in the cold, with the new knife in his right hand and the ash spear on the ground beside him, moving through the slow figures Feng taught him: guard, cover, strike. He stops when he sees her. He does not say anything. He waits.

She stands at the edge of the lamplight. She finds that she has to put her hands behind her back to keep them still.

"I am going to tell you some things," she says. "I am not going to ask you anything."

He nods slowly.

"Tonight Zhao Qian met your uncle at the old shrine. He gave him a powder. It is tasteless and odorless and harmless to a man who sits still. When a cultivator takes in a breakthrough, it stops the heart for one breath. It shatters the foundation. Your uncle is to put a pinch of it on the outside of your grandfather's pill, the day it arrives." Her voice is perfectly level. She is proud of it. "He took it. He wept. He put it in his left cuff."

Lin Jian does not move. His face, in the lamplight, has gone a very still, very grave shade of white.

"The pill arrives at the start of summer," she says. "Mo will bring it, sealed, to your uncle's hands. It goes to your grandfather the same hour. I do not know how it will be done. I do not know how anyone could stop it." She meets his eyes. "I know that I cannot."

He is silent.

"That is all," says Su Qinghe. "That is everything I know."

She turns to go. She gets as far as the gate before she stops, because she has realized, quite suddenly, that she has not breathed in several seconds.

"Jian."

"Yes, Mother."

She does not turn around. She says it to the dark, to the cold, to the rows of sleeping terraces, to the whole indifferent mountain.

"I am not asking if you can."

A long silence, and then, behind her, very softly, the sound of a boy putting a spear down on frozen ground.

"I know," says her son.

She goes in. She does not sleep. But she lies on her back in the dark with her eyes open, listening to the ordinary sounds of her house, and for the first time in a very long while, she is not afraid.
